claim: The 101st Amendment Act, 2016 (assent 8 Sept 2016) inserted Article 246A: Parliament and State Legislatures both have power to make laws on GST 'notwithstanding' Arts 246 and 254; Parliament alone for inter-State supply (246A(2)).
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 279A: the GST Council has the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson, the Union Minister of State for Revenue or Finance, and one Minister nominated by each State Government; it recommends on taxes subsumed, exemptions, model law, threshold, rates and floor rates with bands, calamity rates and special provision for 11 named States.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 279A(9): decisions need three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting; Centre's vote weighs one-third, all States together two-thirds. Under the Council's own rules the States' two-thirds is shared equally: weighted States' vote = (States in favour / States present and voting) x 2/3.
value: Centre 1/3; each State equal share of 2/3
source: GST Council, Rules for conduct of business
page_or_section: Chapter V, rule 15(3) and illustration (PDF pp.13-14, printed pp.9-10)
second_source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
note: Derived: a State of any size has one equal share, so small States count as much as large. The worked example in the rules: 25 States present, 20 States and Centre in favour, carried. Rules say a Member may seek a secret-ballot division (rule 14). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Formula read from page image: WS = (SF/SP) x (2/3); example 1/3 + (20/25)(2/3) = 13/15 carried. Confirmed.

claim: Article 279A(11) requires the Council to establish a mechanism to adjudicate disputes between the Union and States or among States over the Council's recommendations or their implementation.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council
note: Mechanism not found as set up; in Oct 2020 Council debate one State asked to 'activate' it and another said the proposal for an authority had been rejected earlier (see 2020-GS3-12 ledger).

claim: Supreme Court, Mohit Minerals (19 May 2022): Council recommendations are not binding on the Union and States. Reasons: deletion of Art 279B and the structure of Art 279A show 'persuasive value'; neither does 279A begin with a non-obstante clause nor is 246A subject to 279A; to regard them as binding edicts would 'disrupt fiscal federalism', since Union and States hold equal power to legislate on GST.
source: Union of India v Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022, Supreme Court, 19 May 2022 (Court's own copy)
note: Para 148(i)(c): where the Government makes rules under the CGST/IGST Acts it is bound by recommendations. Judgment text writes 'Article 279(1)' for 279A(1).

claim: Court: Indian federalism is a dialogue between cooperative and uncooperative federalism, where federal units may use means of persuasion 'ranging from collaboration to contestation'; the Centre has one-third vote share and Art 246A has no repugnancy clause, so recommendations cannot be binding.
source: Union of India v Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022, Supreme Court, 19 May 2022 (Court's own copy)
page_or_section: Part C para 51 (judgment p.82) and Part E para 148(i)(b) (p.151)
note: First sentence from p.82-83 passage; the quotation about persuasion is from 148(i)(b), p.151. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Pages fixed: one-third vote share and no repugnancy clause are para 51, p.82; the collaboration-to-contestation quote is p.151.

claim: Court on legislative history: the 2011 Amendment Bill had a draft Art 279B for a GST Dispute Settlement Authority and required Council decisions by consensus of all members present; those were not carried into the 2016 Act.
source: Union of India v Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022, Supreme Court, 19 May 2022 (Court's own copy)
page_or_section: Part C paras 32-33 (pp.65-66: draft 279A(8) consensus, draft 279B), para 36 (pp.69-70: Standing Committee drops 279B), para 38 (p.70: deleted in 2014 Bill)
note: Page numbers approximate: the 2011 Bill passage sits in the 'Legislative History' section C.1 (index p.56). Re-check page before printing. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Approximate pages replaced with verified pages. Draft 279A quorum was one-third, consensus of all members present (p.66).

claim: Article 269A: IGST on inter-State supplies and imports is levied and collected by the Government of India and apportioned to the States as Parliament provides on the Council's recommendation; the amount apportioned to a State does not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Section 18 of the 101st Amendment Act: Parliament shall by law, on the Council's recommendation, provide compensation to the States for revenue loss due to GST 'for a period of five years'.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 279A(4)(g) singles out Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Jammu and Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand for special provision, and 279A(4)(f) lets the Council recommend a special rate for a specified period to raise resources in a natural calamity or disaster.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Seventh Schedule: State List entry 52 (entry tax) and entry 55 (advertisements) omitted, entry 54 reduced to sales tax on petroleum crude, HSD, petrol, natural gas, ATF and alcohol; Union List entries 92 and 92C omitted. So States gave up their sales-tax and entry-tax heads and the Union gave up service tax and excise (except 84 goods).
value: States and Union both surrender heads
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Passage and ratification: Rajya Sabha passed the Bill on 3 Aug 2016, Lok Sabha on 8 Aug 2016, 'passed by more than 15 States', assent 8 Sept 2016; Article 279A brought into force from 12 Sept 2016; the Council first met on 22-23 Sept 2016.
Article 279A(6): the Council 'shall be guided by the need for a harmonised structure of goods and services tax and for the development of a harmonised national market for goods and services'.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Council Rules (Chapter V): proposals are 'discussed threadbare', the Chairperson puts the question by show of hands, and any Member can seek a division by secret ballot; the result of a division 'shall not be challenged'.
source: GST Council, Rules for conduct of business
note: Does not say how often divisions are held. Whether any decision has gone to a division is NOT in these sources.

claim: On 3 Sept 2025 the 56th Council (Chair: Union Finance Minister) recommended a 2-rate structure (18% and 5%) plus 40% for a few goods and services, but, for pan masala, gutkha, cigarettes, chewing tobacco and bidi, kept existing GST and compensation cess until compensation-cess loan and interest are discharged.
source: PIB / GST Council: Recommendations of the 56th GST Council meeting, 3 Sept 2025
note: Shows the Council still working by recommendation and the 2020 borrowing still shaping 2025 decisions. Whether the decision was by consensus or division: NOT in this press note.

claim: Compensation: Parliament's duty under s.18 ran for five years; the Compensation Act s.8 provides the cess for 'five years or for such period as may be prescribed on the recommendations of the Council'. In Oct 2020 the Council approved extending the cess beyond June 2022 'till the entire shortfall is covered'.
source: Minutes of the 42nd GST Council meeting, 5 and 12 Oct 2020 (GST Council; OCR text noisy)
second_source: GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 (Act 15 of 2017, assent 12 Apr 2017), text on CBIC GST site
